findings.ref: tests/lib/loop-driver.sh assert_terminal vs design.md per-kind producer table ('done-transition')
findings.note: The emit fires on paths the design does not sanction and is unasserted either way. design.md requires the event 'firing exactly once per round at the instant it evaluates the freshly-read .terminal.state against the loop's expected terminal state' and 'always the last event in the round's own event sub-sequence'. As implemented, the emit runs before the comparison and therefore also records a done-transition on a FAILING terminal assertion (expected != observed still emits), while the two early returns (exit_code != 0, empty expected) emit nothing - so 'exactly once per round' does not hold in either direction. _loop_trace_normalize enforces sequence monotonicity, known producers, and capability-event ordering, but has no rule making done-transition terminal in its sub-sequence, so nothing in the bundle catches this. No test in the bundle exercises assert_terminal's failing or early-return paths against a trace.

Twin comparison semantics differ: bash '[[ "$expected" == "$observed" ]]' is case-sensitive, while PowerShell 'return ($expected -eq $Observed)' is case-insensitive. The sibling Test-CapabilityApplicability correctly uses '-ceq', and TEST-009.7 asserts case-sensitivity for applicability but nothing equivalent exists for the terminal state. A mis-cased observed terminal state passes in PowerShell and fails in bash. The divergence predates this task, but AC-009 as re-baselined now purports to lock assert_terminal's 'expected/observed comparison semantics', which the twins do not in fact share.
